newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurds flee to Iran, Baghdad-backed KDP celebrates.
newsitem.headline: Kurds flee to Iran, Baghdad-backed KDP celebrates.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Kurds fled towards Iran on Tuesday as a Baghdad-backed militia celebrated the takeover of northern Iraq's biggest city, the last stronghold of its longtime Kurdish rival.
"The number is between 70,000 and 75,000 we believe," said a United Nations official in Arbil, the capital of Kurdish northern Iraq.

A U.N. refugee official in Tehran said he had reports an unspecified number of refugees were crossing the border to Iran. He said they were headed for Iran's west Azerbaijan province and Marivan border areas.

The Iranian news agency IRNA, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, quoted loval Iranian officials sa saying nearly 3,000 had arrived at two border posts, asking for food, medicine and medical care for pregnant women and the sick. Iranian authorities were providing water and other basic needs.

The Iraqi-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) swept through northern Iraq on a nine-day drive that climaxed on Monday with the capture from the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) of Sulaimaniya, population one million.
"More than 50,000 people have left the city," said a U.N. official. "We have to get to work to get them back."

The success of the KDP, backed by Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, has raised the spectre of a repeat of a 1991 exodus when more an estimated two million Kurds poured into Turkey and Iran for fear Saddam would use poison gas against them.
Iraq launched a gas attack on Halabja, near Sulaimaniya, in 1988 after Kurdish rebels aided Iranian forces in the area during the eight-year Iran-Iraq war.
In Sulaimaniya, thousands of KDP guerrillas drove around the city, waving flags. Patriotic music blared from loudspeakers. Some buildings were on fire, but there was little sign of heavy fighting.
U.N. officials said they would provide medical supplies to the refugees to fight dysentery, but said they had no intention of providing food or tents that would create camps.
KDP guerrillas said they took Sulaimaniya, the last PUK stronghold, on Monday evening after launching a a surprise attack from Halabja to the southeast without waiting for orders.

"We entered the city at 7 o'clock (1500 GMT). We started from Halabja," said Raof Payzani, 28. "Some units advanced without orders. Part of our KDP contingent was from Sulaimaniya. They didn't want to wait."
"They (the PUK) ran away immediately without any resistance when they saw the great superiority of our forces," he said.
Before the attack the PUK burned its headquarters, ammunition dumps and its members' homes to deny the KDP the opportunity of looting them, a senior U.N. official said.
"Capturing symbols is what it is all about. Burning them, looting them and putting them on TV," he said.
Officials in Iran, 50 km (30 miles) from Sulaimaniya, called for international aid to handle a possible refugee influx.

"Iranian officials are very alarmed and envisage hundreds of thousands of refugees pouring in over the border," said Laurens Jolles, an official of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) office in Tehran.
He said Iran had asked international organisations to be ready for any situation "which might be a parallel to 1991".
More than a million Iraqis, most of them Kurds, poured through the mountains to Iran when Baghdad crushed Kurdish and Shi'ite Moslem uprisings which erupted after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War.
Most of the Kurds returned to northern Iraq after the Western allies set up a safe haven and began regular air patrols to shield civilians from any attack by Baghdad.
Washington launched missile attacks on southern Iraq after tens of thousands of Iraqi government troops helped the KDP capture the city of Arbil on August 31.
